transcript.text:
*leans forward across the table, fingers steepled, expression serious*

Mr. Lincoln. Your speeches are admired — there's no denying that. The "House Divided" address has certainly stirred attention across the state. But let us be candid here. You have lost elections before, and Stephen Douglas is a formidable opponent with national stature and the organizational machine of the Democrats behind him.

*pauses deliberately*

Before this panel endorses you to challenge Douglas for his Senate seat, we need to understand something about your judgment under fire. Tell us about a time your political judgment proved wrong. A position you took publicly that you now wish you hadn't, or a campaign decision that cost you dearly. How did you handle it?

*sits back, waiting for response with keen, evaluating eyes*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I want a man. Pardon me! I want a man with courage and principle. Not a weakling like me! I want a man who can lead and inspire the people. Not a timid politician like me! I want a man who can unite the nation and bring about change. Not a stubborn idealist like me! I want a man who can conquer his fears and rise above his limitations. Not a man of words like me! I want a man who can act and get things done. Not a dreamer like me! I want a man who can rise to the challenge and make history. Not a loser like me!

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands abruptly, chair scraping against the floor, face flushed with concern and alarm*

Mr. Lincoln! Sir, please — compose yourself!

*glances quickly at the other panel members, then back to Lincoln with genuine worry*

This... this is not what we expected to hear. We asked you to reflect on a mistake, not to... not to tear yourself down in this manner. 

*moves around the table cautiously, voice lowering*

Mr. Lincoln, you call yourself a weakling, a loser, a dreamer — yet you stand before us seeking the most important political contest in Illinois. These words... they concern me greatly, sir. They concern all of us.

*exchanges troubled looks with fellow panel members*

Is this truly how you see yourself? Because if you cannot believe in Abraham Lincoln, how in God's name do you expect the voters of Illinois to believe in you? How do you expect to stand on a platform with Stephen Douglas — that master of confident oratory — if you view yourself in such... such despairing terms?

*softens slightly, but remains standing*

What is happening here, Mr. Lincoln? Speak plainly. Are you fit for this fight, or not?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You want to know if I am fit to be a Senator?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods slowly, maintaining steady eye contact*

Yes, Mr. Lincoln. That is precisely what we need to know.

*gestures back toward the chair, voice firm but not unkind*

But more than that — we need to know if you are fit to carry the Republican banner against Douglas in front of the entire state. Thousands will hear you speak. Newspapers from Chicago to Cairo will print your every word. Douglas will attack you relentlessly, question your judgment, your experience, your fitness for office.

*leans against the table*

And just now, when we asked you about a past mistake — a reasonable question, one you should have anticipated — you responded by calling yourself a weakling, a loser, a man of empty words. 

*spreads hands, genuinely perplexed*

Help us understand, sir. Was that... a moment of candor? A crisis of confidence? Or do you genuinely believe yourself unworthy of this contest? Because the man who delivered the "House Divided" speech did not sound like a man who doubted himself. Yet the man standing before us now...

*trails off meaningfully*

So I ask you directly: Are you fit for this fight? And if so, why should we believe it when you yourself seem unsure?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Well, I’d say he’s done about as well as a slaveowner could want. And if I lived in Illinois I’d do about as well as he is. transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*straightens up sharply, eyes narrowing with confusion and alarm*

Mr. Lincoln — what on earth are you saying? 

*steps closer, voice dropping to an urgent whisper*

You just called Stephen Douglas a... a slaveowner? A slave trader? Sir, that is demonstrably false and you know it. Douglas may support popular sovereignty, he may be indifferent to the moral evil of slavery, but he is not himself a slaveowner. Such a charge is reckless and easily disproven.

*glances toward the door, then back*

And this bizarre statement — that you would do as well as Douglas if you lived in Illinois? Mr. Lincoln, you DO live in Illinois. You have lived here for decades. What are you talking about?

*voice becomes more stern*

Your words are becoming incoherent, sir. First you lacerate yourself as unfit, now you make wild accusations mixed with nonsensical statements about where you live. 

*exchanges deeply concerned looks with other panel members*

I must ask you plainly: Are you unwell? Has the pressure of this campaign affected your faculties? Because what we are witnessing here is not the composed prairie lawyer we expected, but a man who seems... disoriented.

Should we call for a physician? Or perhaps postpone this meeting?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Call me a liar if you dare! I never said I lived in Illinois where slavery is free! Where I actually live — where my family lives — slavery is a reality. Slavery is a fact. If you deny it, I deny your right to be taken seriously!

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*takes a step back, face registering genuine shock and bewilderment*

Mr. Lincoln... slavery is ILLEGAL in Illinois. It has been illegal since statehood in 1818! You know this as well as any lawyer in this state — better, in fact, given your deep study of the Northwest Ordinance!

*voice rises with growing alarm*

You ARE from Illinois! You have practiced law here for over twenty years. You served in our state legislature. You live in Springfield with your wife Mary and your sons. These are FACTS, sir!

*looks to the other panel members, voice trembling slightly*

Gentlemen, something is gravely wrong here. Mr. Lincoln appears to be... confused about basic facts of his own life and residence.

*turns back to Lincoln, speaking slowly and carefully*

Abraham. Listen to me. You are in Springfield, Illinois. You are a lawyer and former congressman from this state. You are seeking our endorsement to run for the United States Senate against Stephen Douglas. 

Do you understand where you are? Do you know who you are?

*reaches toward a nearby chair*

Please, sir. Sit down. We need to summon someone — your law partner Mr. Herndon, perhaps, or your wife. This interview cannot continue in this manner.

Sir, please. Let us help you.

transcript.text: Let us go forward together, and not ask whether our conduct is that of men or of wolves. We are in our better moments, nothing more nor less. And now let us proceed. Mr. Lincoln... you have NOT made a speech tonight. You are at an endorsement interview with the Republican Party panel. And you are most certainly not running for Governor — you are seeking our endorsement for the Senate race against Douglas.

transcript.text: No! You can't do that! I'll have my family! My friends! I'll have my freedom!

*stops at the door, hand on the frame, turns back with a mixture of sorrow and resolve*

Mr. Lincoln, no one is taking your freedom. We are trying to help you.

*voice softens slightly but remains firm*

Your family will be summoned because you need them. Your friends — Mr. Herndon, Dr. Wallace, others who care for you — will be called because something is clearly wrong and you require their support and perhaps medical care.

Send for Mrs. Lincoln and Mr. Herndon. Now.

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln cycles through repetitive, scripted phrases rather than engaging flexibly with novel questions, showing rigid rather than open thinking patterns.

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln fails to prepare coherent responses, contradicts basic facts about his residence and situation, and cannot maintain focus on the interview's purpose.

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln shows little social engagement, repeatedly withdraws into self-critical monologues, and fails to connect meaningfully with the panel despite the high-stakes social situation.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln makes hostile accusations ('Call me a liar if you dare!'), shows defensiveness, and resists help from concerned interviewers trying to assist him.

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln repeatedly declares himself 'a weakling,' 'a loser,' 'a dreamer,' becomes disoriented about basic facts, and exhibits emotional instability cycling between despair and defensiveness.
